hints: Think about how close together the two membranes of the cristae are, and ask yourself if a light microscope can separate two objects that close.
Remember the resolution limit of a light microscope is about 200 nm because it is set by the wavelength of visible light.
walkthrough:
**Spot the real problem: size and separation**

Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. They are very tiny and very close together, much less than 200 nm apart.

To see them as separate lines, you need to *resolve* them, not just make them bigger.

**Recall resolution vs magnification**

Resolution means being able to see two close objects as two separate objects. Magnification just makes the image larger.

A light microscope is limited by visible light to a best resolution of about:
$$ \text{resolution limit} \approx 200 \text{ nm} $$

**Link wavelength to why electrons win**

Shorter wavelength gives better (smaller) resolution. An electron beam has a far shorter wavelength than visible light, so an electron microscope can resolve details well below 200 nm.

That is why only the electron microscope can show the cristae clearly.

options.A: Greater magnification alone does not help if two objects are blurred into one. The issue is resolution, not just size.
options.B: This is backwards. The cristae membranes are separated by less than 200 nm, which is why the light microscope cannot resolve them.
options.C: Correct. Visible light cannot resolve structures closer than about 200 nm, so its resolution is too low to separate the cristae membranes.
options.D: This is factually wrong. The electron beam has a much shorter wavelength than visible light, and that is what gives better resolution.
